excerpt: We will maintain the position of Responsible Scaling Officer, a designated member of staff who is responsible for reducing catastrophic risk, primarily by ensuring this policy is designed and implemented effectively.
paraphrase: Anthropic commits to maintaining a Responsible Scaling Officer role responsible for reducing catastrophic risk through effective policy implementation.

context_stem: The Responsible Scaling Officer's duties will include (but are not limited to):
excerpt: (1) as needed, proposing updates to this policy to the Board of Directors; (2) approving relevant model training or deployment decisions based on capability and safeguard assessments; (3) reviewing major contracts (i.e., deployment partnerships) for consistency with this policy;
paraphrase: The RSO's duties include proposing policy updates, approving training/deployment decisions, and reviewing major contracts for policy consistency.

context_stem: The Responsible Scaling Officer's duties will include (but are not limited to):
excerpt: (4) overseeing implementation of this policy, including the allocation of sufficient resources; (5) receiving and addressing reports of potential instances of noncompliance; (6) promptly notifying the Board of Directors of any cases of noncompliance that pose material risk; and (7) making judgment calls on policy interpretation and application.
paraphrase: The RSO's duties also include overseeing implementation and resourcing, handling noncompliance reports, notifying the Board of material risk, and interpreting the policy.

excerpt: We will develop internal safety procedures for incident scenarios. Such scenarios include (1) pausing training in response to reaching Capability Thresholds; (2) responding to a security incident involving model weights; and (3) responding to severe jailbreaks or vulnerabilities in deployed models, including restricting access in safety emergencies that cannot otherwise be mitigated.
paraphrase: Anthropic will create internal procedures for handling incidents such as pausing training, security breaches of model weights, and severe jailbreaks.

excerpt: We will run exercises to ensure our readiness for incident scenarios.
paraphrase: Anthropic will conduct exercises to test readiness for incident scenarios.

excerpt: We will share summaries of Capability Reports and Safeguards Reports with Anthropic's regular-clearance staff, redacting any highly-sensitive information.
paraphrase: Anthropic will share redacted summaries of Capability and Safeguards Reports with regular-clearance staff.

excerpt: We will share a minimally redacted version of these reports with a subset of staff, to help us surface relevant technical safety considerations.
paraphrase: A subset of staff will receive a minimally redacted version of the reports to help surface safety considerations.

excerpt: For each Capabilities or Safeguards Report, we will solicit feedback from internal teams with visibility into the relevant activities, with the aims of informing future refinements to our methodology and, in some circumstances, identifying weaknesses and informing the CEO and RSO's decisions.
paraphrase: Anthropic will seek internal feedback on each Capabilities or Safeguards Report to refine methodology and inform decisions.

excerpt: We will maintain a process through which Anthropic staff may anonymously notify the Responsible Scaling Officer of any potential instances of noncompliance with this policy.
paraphrase: Anthropic will maintain an anonymous reporting process for staff to notify the RSO of potential noncompliance.

excerpt: We will also establish a policy governing noncompliance reporting, which will (1) protect reporters from retaliation and (2) set forth a mechanism for escalating reports to one or more members of the Board of Directors in cases where the report relates to conduct of the Responsible Scaling Officer.
paraphrase: Anthropic will establish a noncompliance reporting policy that protects reporters and provides escalation to the Board when the RSO is implicated.

excerpt: Further, we will track and investigate any reported or otherwise identified potential instances of noncompliance with this policy. Where reports are substantiated, we will take appropriate and proportional corrective action and document the same.
paraphrase: Anthropic will track, investigate, and take documented corrective action on substantiated noncompliance instances.

excerpt: The Responsible Scaling Officer will regularly update the Board of Directors on substantial cases of noncompliance and overall trends.
paraphrase: The RSO will provide regular Board updates on substantial noncompliance cases and trends.

excerpt: In addition to noncompliance processes, we will (1) establish pathways for Anthropic staff to raise any issues related to this policy, including the overall risk levels of our models and implementation challenges; and (2) regularly review our compliance with this policy's procedural requirements.
paraphrase: Beyond noncompliance channels, Anthropic will create pathways for staff to raise policy concerns and will regularly review procedural compliance.

excerpt: Cases deemed to present minimal additional risk may be reported to the Board in quarterly summary reports.
paraphrase: Low-risk noncompliance cases may be reported via quarterly summaries instead of immediately.

excerpt: In cases where this policy is unintentionally ambiguous, we will act in accordance with the Responsible Scaling Officer or CEO's judgment, and aim to clarify the ambiguity in the next policy update.
paraphrase: Ambiguities will be resolved via RSO or CEO judgment, with clarification intended in the next update.

excerpt: We will not impose contractual non-disparagement obligations on employees, candidates, or former employees in a way that could impede or discourage them from publicly raising safety concerns about Anthropic.
paraphrase: Anthropic will not use non-disparagement clauses to prevent staff from raising public safety concerns.

excerpt: If we offer agreements with a non-disparagement clause, that clause will not preclude raising safety concerns, nor will it preclude disclosure of the existence of that clause.
paraphrase: Any non-disparagement clauses offered will not block raising safety concerns or disclosing the clause's existence.

excerpt: Changes to this policy will be proposed by the CEO and the Responsible Scaling Officer and approved by the Board of Directors, in consultation with the Long-Term Benefit Trust.
paraphrase: Policy changes are proposed by the CEO and RSO and approved by the Board, in consultation with the Long-Term Benefit Trust.

excerpt: The current version of the RSP is accessible at www.anthropic.com/rsp. We will update the public version of the RSP before any changes take effect and record any differences from the prior draft in a change log.
paraphrase: The RSP is publicly accessible online, and updates will be published before taking effect with a change log documenting differences.

excerpt: It is possible at some point in the future that another actor in the frontier AI ecosystem will pass, or be on track to imminently pass, a Capability Threshold without implementing measures equivalent to the Required Safeguards such that their actions pose a serious risk for the world.
paraphrase: A future scenario could occur where another AI actor surpasses a Capability Threshold without equivalent safeguards, posing serious global risk.

excerpt: In such a scenario, because the incremental increase in risk attributable to us would be small, we might decide to lower the Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: In that scenario, Anthropic might lower Required Safeguards since its own incremental risk contribution would be small.

excerpt: If we take this measure, however, we will also acknowledge the overall level of risk posed by AI systems (including ours), and will invest significantly in making a case to the U.S. government for taking regulatory action to mitigate such risk to acceptable levels.
paraphrase: If safeguards are lowered under this scenario, Anthropic will acknowledge overall AI risk and advocate for U.S. government regulatory action.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: We will publicly release key information related to the evaluation and deployment of our models (not including sensitive details).
paraphrase: Anthropic will publicly release key model evaluation and deployment information, excluding sensitive details.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: These include summaries of related Capability and Safeguards reports when we deploy a model as well as plans for current and future comprehensive capability assessments and deployment and security safeguards.
paraphrase: Public disclosures include report summaries at deployment and plans for capability assessments and safeguards.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: We will also periodically release information on internal reports of potential instances of non-compliance and other implementation challenges we encounter.
paraphrase: Anthropic will periodically release information about noncompliance reports and implementation challenges.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: We will solicit input from external experts in relevant domains in the process of developing and conducting capability and safeguards assessments.
paraphrase: Anthropic will seek external expert input while developing and conducting capability and safeguards assessments.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: We may also solicit external expert input prior to making final decisions on the capability and safeguards assessments.
paraphrase: Anthropic may also seek external input before finalizing capability and safeguards assessment decisions.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: We will notify a relevant U.S. Government entity if a model requires stronger protections than the ASL-2 Standard.
paraphrase: Anthropic will notify a relevant U.S. Government entity when a model requires stronger-than-ASL-2 protections.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: On approximately an annual basis, we will commission a third-party review that assesses whether we adhered to this policy's main procedural commitments (we expect to iterate on the exact list since this has not been done before for RSPs).
paraphrase: Anthropic will commission an annual third-party review of procedural compliance with the policy, expecting to refine the review's scope over time.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: This review will focus on procedural compliance, not substantive outcomes. We will also do such reviews internally on a more regular cadence.
paraphrase: The third-party review addresses procedure not outcomes, and similar reviews will also be done internally more frequently.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: We currently expect that if we do not deploy the model publicly and instead proceed with training or limited deployments, we will likely instead share evaluation details with a relevant U.S. Government entity.
paraphrase: For non-public deployments, Anthropic expects to share evaluation details with a U.S. Government entity instead.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: These will be posted to www.anthropic.com/rsp-updates. We anticipate providing updates at least every 6-12 months.
paraphrase: Updates will be posted online, anticipated at least every 6-12 months.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: Where possible, we will include descriptions of the empirical evaluation results we believe would indicate that a model is no longer safe to store under the ASL-2 Standard.
paraphrase: Updates will where possible describe evaluation results indicating a model is no longer safe under ASL-2.

section_heading: 7. Governance and Transparency / 7.2. Transparency and External Input
excerpt: Our purpose in these updates is to provide sufficient detail to facilitate conversations about best practices for safeguards, capability evaluations, and elicitation.
paraphrase: The intent of these updates is to enable dialogue about best practices in safeguards and evaluation.

excerpt: Technical and operational standards for safely training and deploying frontier AI models. Higher ASLs correspond to stronger safety and security measures required for more capable models.
paraphrase: ASLs are standards for safe training/deployment, with higher levels requiring stronger safeguards for more capable models.

excerpt: The current default standard for all Anthropic models, including security measures, safety testing, and automated misuse detection.
paraphrase: ASL-2 is the baseline standard for all Anthropic models covering security, safety testing, and misuse detection.

excerpt: A higher level of safeguards required when a model cannot be certified as ASL-2 appropriate. It includes more stringent security and deployment measures designed to mitigate risks from more capable models.
paraphrase: ASL-3 applies when a model cannot be certified ASL-2 appropriate, requiring stricter security and deployment measures.

excerpt: A document attesting that a model is sufficiently far from each of the relevant Capability Thresholds, and therefore (still) appropriate for storing under an ASL-N Standard. It includes evaluation procedures, results, and other relevant evidence gathered around the time of testing.
paraphrase: A Capability Report is documentation showing a model remains sufficiently distant from Capability Thresholds, including evaluation details.

excerpt: Specific AI capabilities that, if reached, would require stronger safeguards than the current baseline ASL-N standard provides.
paraphrase: Capability Thresholds are specific capabilities that trigger the need for stronger safeguards.

excerpt: A scaling trend-based metric that accounts for both FLOPs and algorithmic improvements.
paraphrase: Effective Compute is a metric combining FLOPs and algorithmic improvements to track scaling trends.

excerpt: Empirical tests designed to provide early warning when a model is approaching a Capability Threshold. These tests are intended to trigger before a model actually reaches a dangerous capability.
paraphrase: Evaluations are tests meant to give early warning before a model reaches a dangerous capability.

excerpt: Floating-Point Operation(s). The amount of computation required to train or run a model. The number of FLOPs can be used as one indicator of a model's computational complexity and, indirectly, its potential capabilities.
paraphrase: FLOPs measure the computation required to train/run a model and indicate computational complexity and potential capability.

excerpt: Anthropic's Board of Directors approves the RSP and receives Capability Reports and Safeguards Reports. The LTBT is an external body that is consulted on policy changes and also provided with Capability Reports and Safeguards Reports. More details about the LTBT are available here.
paraphrase: The Board approves the RSP and receives reports; the LTBT is an external body consulted on policy changes and also given the reports.

excerpt: The standard of safety and security measures that must be implemented when a model reaches a Capability Threshold.
paraphrase: Required Safeguards are the safety/security measures mandated once a Capability Threshold is reached.

excerpt: A designated staff member responsible for reducing catastrophic risk, primarily by ensuring this policy is designed and implemented effectively. Their duties include reviewing policy updates, approving reports, overseeing implementation, and approving deployments.
paraphrase: The RSO is a staff member tasked with reducing catastrophic risk via policy design/implementation, report approval, and deployment sign-off.

excerpt: A document attesting that the implemented safeguards meet an ASL-N Standard. It details the design and planned implementation of safeguards, and evidence to demonstrate their expected effectiveness.
paraphrase: A Safeguards Report documents that implemented safeguards meet an ASL-N standard with supporting evidence.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 1
excerpt: Acceptable use policies and model cards: Publication of model cards for significant new models describing capabilities, limitations, evaluations, and intended use cases.
paraphrase: ASL-2 deployment requires publishing model cards describing capabilities, limitations, evaluations, and use cases for significant new models.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 1
excerpt: Enforcement of a Usage Policy that restricts, at a minimum, catastrophic and high harm use cases, including using the model to generate content that could cause severe risks to the continued existence of humankind, or direct and severe harm to individuals.
paraphrase: ASL-2 requires enforcing a Usage Policy prohibiting at minimum catastrophic and high-harm use cases.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 2
excerpt: Harmlessness training and automated detection: Training models to refuse requests to aid in causing harm, such as with Constitutional AI or other improved techniques, and the use of model enhanced trust and safety detection and enforcement.
paraphrase: ASL-2 requires harmlessness training (e.g., Constitutional AI) and model-enhanced trust and safety detection/enforcement.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 3
excerpt: Fine-tuning protections: In finetuning products, data is filtered for harmfulness, and models are subject to automated evaluation to check harmlessness features are not degraded.
paraphrase: Finetuning products must filter harmful data and undergo automated checks that harmlessness features remain intact.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 3
excerpt: There are a very limited number of use cases where this tooling is disabled. These are negotiated on a case by case basis and considered only for extremely low risk use cases that involve company personnel.
paraphrase: A very limited number of low-risk, personnel-only use cases may disable this tooling, negotiated case by case.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Deployment Standard / item 4
excerpt: Vulnerability reporting channels: Clearly indicated paths within the product for users to report harmful or dangerous model outputs, as well as a bug bounty for universal jailbreaks.
paraphrase: ASL-2 requires clear in-product vulnerability reporting channels and a bug bounty for universal jailbreaks.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / intro
excerpt: ASL-2 Security Standard: A security system that can likely thwart most opportunistic attackers.
paraphrase: The ASL-2 Security Standard is designed to thwart most opportunistic attackers.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 1
excerpt: Supply chain: Vendor and supplier security must be regularly reviewed to ensure that they meet security standards. Software updates should be frequently managed and compliance monitoring automated where possible.
paraphrase: Supply chain security requires regular vendor reviews, frequent software update management, and automated compliance monitoring.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 2
excerpt: Offices: Physical security should entail visitor access logs and restrictions protect on-site assets. Highly sensitive interactions should utilize advanced authentication like security keys.
paraphrase: Office security should include visitor logs, asset access restrictions, and advanced authentication for sensitive interactions.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 2
excerpt: Network visibility should be maintained and office access controls and communications should maximize on-site protections.
paraphrase: Network visibility and office access controls should be maintained to maximize on-site protections.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 3
excerpt: Workforce: People-critical processes must represent a key aspect of cybersecurity. Mandatory periodic infosec training educates all employees on secure practices, like proper system configurations and strong passwords, and fosters a proactive "security mindset."
paraphrase: Workforce security requires people-focused processes and mandatory periodic infosec training fostering a security mindset.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 3
excerpt: Fundamental infrastructure and policies promoting secure-by-design and secure-by-default principles should be incorporated into the engineering process. An insider risk program should tie access to job roles. Rapid incident response protocols must be deployed.
paraphrase: Secure-by-design/default principles should be embedded in engineering, insider risk should be tied to job roles, and rapid incident response is required.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 4
excerpt: Compartmentalization: Segmented system isolation must ensure limited blast radius. Features like zero trust architecture should require access from approved devices.
paraphrase: Compartmentalization requires segmented isolation limiting blast radius and zero trust architecture restricting access to approved devices.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 4
excerpt: Strict protocols must be deployed to regulate weight copies on company networks and limit storage to only approved, restricted systems.
paraphrase: Strict protocols must govern weight copies on company networks, limiting storage to approved restricted systems.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 5
excerpt: Infrastructure: Standard security infrastructure, monitoring software, access management tools, and disk encryption provide a technology baseline. Process elements like incident reporting procedures, lost/stolen device protocols and Detection and Response should support these.
paraphrase: Infrastructure baseline includes standard security tools, monitoring, access management and disk encryption, supported by incident and device-loss protocols.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 5
excerpt: External validation like SOC 2 compliance and continuous vulnerability management must ensure adaptations match infosec developments. Programs like bug bounties and vulnerability discovery should incentivize exposing flaws.
paraphrase: External validation (e.g., SOC 2) and continuous vulnerability management must keep pace with infosec developments, supported by bug bounty programs.

locator: App B / ASL-2 Security Standard / item 6
excerpt: Operations: Ongoing configuration management, compliance drills, integrated security approaches and mandatory external reviews should embed security within regular operations and harden processes during organizational changes.
paraphrase: Operational security requires ongoing configuration management, compliance drills, and mandatory external reviews to embed security and harden processes during change.

excerpt: This appendix contains detailed definitions for each Capability Threshold in Section 2.
paraphrase: The appendix provides detailed definitions of each Capability Threshold referenced in Section 2.

context_stem: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons:
excerpt: CBRN-3: The ability to significantly assist individuals or groups with basic STEM backgrounds in obtaining, producing, or deploying CBRN weapons.
paraphrase: CBRN-3 is the capability to significantly help STEM-background actors obtain, produce, or deploy CBRN weapons.

excerpt: We assess this by comparing what potential attackers could achieve with full model access versus 2023-level online resources, assuming they have funding and up to one year of time to invest, but no initial specialized expertise.
paraphrase: Assessment compares model-assisted attacker capability against 2023-level online resources, assuming funding and up to one year, but no prior specialized expertise.

context_stem: Chemical, Biological, Radiological, and Nuclear (CBRN) weapons:
excerpt: CBRN-4: The ability to substantially uplift CBRN development capabilities of moderately resourced state programs (with relevant expert teams), such as by novel weapons design, substantially accelerating existing processes, or dramatic reduction in technical barriers.
paraphrase: CBRN-4 is the ability to substantially advance state-level CBRN programs via novel design, acceleration, or barrier reduction.

excerpt: We currently define this as uplifting a team of people with skills equivalent to entry-level PhD biologists to be able to approximate the capabilities of a world-class, state-backed bioweapons team.
paraphrase: CBRN-4 is currently defined as uplifting entry-level PhD-equivalent biologists to approximate world-class state-backed bioweapons team capability.
stated_bar: entry-level PhD biologists to world-class state-backed bioweapons team

excerpt: AI R&D-4: The ability to fully automate the work of an entry-level, remote-only Researcher at Anthropic.
paraphrase: AI R&D-4 is the ability to fully automate an entry-level, remote-only Anthropic researcher's work.

excerpt: AI R&D-5: The ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling. Specifically, this would be the case if we observed or projected an increase in the effective training compute of the world's most capable model that, over the course of a year, was equivalent to two years of the average rate of progress during the period of early 2018 to early 2024.
paraphrase: AI R&D-5 is the ability to dramatically accelerate scaling, defined as achieving in one year an increase equivalent to two years of the 2018-2024 average progress rate.

excerpt: We roughly estimate that the 2018-2024 average scaleup was around 35x per year, so this would imply an actual or projected one-year scaleup of 352 = ~1000x.
paraphrase: The estimated 35x/year average scaleup implies AI R&D-5 corresponds to a roughly 1000x one-year scaleup.

excerpt: Model Autonomy checkpoint: The ability to perform a wide range of advanced software engineering tasks autonomously that could be precursors to full autonomous replication or automated AI R&D, and that would take a domain expert human 2-8 hours to complete.
paraphrase: The Model Autonomy checkpoint is autonomous performance of advanced software engineering tasks taking a human expert 2-8 hours, as precursors to fuller autonomy.

excerpt: We primarily view this level of model autonomy as a checkpoint on the way to managing the risks of robust, fully autonomous systems with capabilities that might include (a) automating and greatly accelerating research and development in AI development (b) generating their own revenue and using it to run copies of themselves in large-scale, hard-to-shut-down operations.
paraphrase: This autonomy level is viewed as an intermediate checkpoint toward managing risks from fully autonomous systems capable of accelerating AI R&D or self-funding replication.

excerpt: We are uncertain how to choose a specific threshold, but we maintain a current list of specific CBRN capabilities of concern for which we would implement stronger mitigations.
paraphrase: Anthropic maintains a list of specific concerning CBRN capabilities warranting stronger mitigations, despite uncertainty on precise thresholds.

excerpt: We treat these lists as sensitive, but we plan to share them with organizations such as AI Safety Institutes and the Frontier Model Forum, and keep these lists updated.
paraphrase: These sensitive lists will be shared with bodies like AI Safety Institutes and the Frontier Model Forum and kept updated.

excerpt: This comparison is hard to make in practice; this note is to clarify the meaning of the conceptual threshold and the fact that this policy aims to measure risk relative to the world in 2023, so that we can understand how much risk the current generations of frontier models are creating.
paraphrase: This footnote clarifies that the comparison is difficult in practice, and the policy intends to measure risk relative to a 2023 baseline.

excerpt: The 35x/year scaleup estimate is based on assuming the rate of increase in compute being used to train frontier models from ~2018 to May 2024 is 4.2 x/year (reference), the impact of increased (LLM) algorithmic efficiency is roughly equivalent to a further 2.8 x/year (reference), and the impact of post training enhancements is a further 3 x/year (informal estimate).
paraphrase: The 35x/year estimate derives from combining 4.2x/year compute growth, 2.8x/year algorithmic efficiency gains, and 3x/year post-training enhancement gains.

excerpt: Combined, these have an effective rate of scaling of 35 x/year.
paraphrase: The combined effective scaling rate from all three factors is 35x per year.

excerpt: September 19, 2023 (RSP v1.0) RSP-2023 (aka RSP v1.0): Initial version.
paraphrase: The changelog records that the initial RSP version was released September 19, 2023.

excerpt: RSP-2024: This update introduces a more flexible and nuanced approach to assessing and managing AI risks while maintaining our commitment not to train or deploy models unless we have implemented adequate safeguards.
paraphrase: The 2024 update adopts a more flexible risk-management approach while retaining the commitment against training/deploying without adequate safeguards.

excerpt: Key improvements include new capability thresholds to indicate when we should upgrade our safeguards, refined processes for evaluating model capabilities and the adequacy of our safeguards (inspired by safety case methodologies), and new measures for internal governance and external input.
paraphrase: Key 2024 improvements include new capability thresholds, refined safety-case-inspired evaluation processes, and new governance and external-input measures.

excerpt: ASL definition changed: The term "ASL" now refers to groups of technical and operational safeguards (it previously also referred to models). We also introduced the new concepts of Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: The ASL definition was changed to refer only to safeguard groups, no longer to models, alongside new Capability Thresholds and Required Safeguards concepts.

excerpt: This change allows for more targeted application of safeguards based on specific capabilities, rather than broad model categories.
paraphrase: The redefinition enables safeguards to be targeted at specific capabilities rather than broad model categories.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
excerpt: ARA threshold now a checkpoint: We replaced our previous autonomous replication and adaption (ARA) threshold with a "checkpoint" for autonomous AI capabilities.
paraphrase: The previous ARA threshold was replaced with a checkpoint concept for autonomous AI capabilities.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
excerpt: Rather than triggering higher safety standards automatically, reaching this checkpoint will prompt additional evaluation of the model's capabilities and accelerate our preparation of stronger safeguards.
paraphrase: Reaching the checkpoint prompts additional evaluation and accelerated safeguard preparation rather than automatically triggering higher standards.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
excerpt: We previously considered these capabilities as a trigger for increased safeguards, motivated by an attempt to establish some threshold while we developed a better sense of potential threats.
paraphrase: These capabilities were previously treated as a safeguard trigger as a provisional measure while understanding of threats developed.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / ARA threshold now a checkpoint
excerpt: We now believe that these capabilities - at the levels we initially considered - would not necessitate the ASL-3 standard.
paraphrase: Anthropic now believes these capability levels do not require the ASL-3 standard.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / AI R&D threshold added
excerpt: AI R&D threshold added: We added a new threshold for AI systems that can significantly advance AI development.
paraphrase: A new threshold was added for AI systems capable of significantly advancing AI development.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / AI R&D threshold added
excerpt: Such capabilities could lead to rapid, unpredictable advances in AI, potentially outpacing our ability to evaluate and address emerging risks, and may also serve as an early warning sign for the ability to automate R&D in other domains.
paraphrase: These capabilities risk rapid unpredictable AI advances outpacing risk evaluation, and may signal broader R&D automation potential.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
excerpt: Testing for Capability Thresholds: Rather than using prespecified evaluations, we now require an affirmative case that models are sufficiently far from Capability Thresholds.
paraphrase: Anthropic now requires an affirmative case of sufficient distance from Capability Thresholds rather than relying on prespecified evaluations.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
excerpt: Predefined tests may miss emerging risks or be overly conservative relative to the actual threshold of concern.
paraphrase: Predefined tests risk missing emerging risks or being overly conservative relative to actual thresholds.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Testing for Capability Thresholds
excerpt: Our most accurate tests change frequently enough that it is more practical to use this new approach than to have our Board of Directors pre-approve evaluations.
paraphrase: Frequently changing best tests make the new affirmative-case approach more practical than Board pre-approval of evaluations.

excerpt: Adjusted evaluation cadence: We adjusted the comprehensive assessment cadence to 4x Effective Compute or six months of accumulated post-training enhancements (this was previously three months).
paraphrase: The assessment cadence was adjusted to 4x Effective Compute or six months of accumulated post-training enhancements, up from three months.

excerpt: We found that a three-month cadence forced teams to prioritize conducting frequent evaluations over more comprehensive testing and improving methodologies.
paraphrase: A three-month cadence had forced teams to prioritize evaluation frequency over comprehensiveness and methodology improvement.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
excerpt: Less prescriptive evaluation methodology: We have replaced some specifics in our previous testing methodology (e.g., using 1% of compute for elicitation or creating a 6x buffer), with more general requirements to (a) match expected efforts of potential adversaries and (b) provide informal estimates of how further scaling and research developments will impact model capabilities and performance on the same tasks.
paraphrase: Specific prior methodology elements (e.g., 1% compute for elicitation, 6x buffer) were replaced with general requirements to match adversary effort and estimate future capability impacts.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
excerpt: We have found that specific methodologies may become outdated when new research developments are introduced.
paraphrase: Specific methodologies risk becoming outdated as new research emerges.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Less prescriptive evaluation methodology
excerpt: Although still an aspirational goal, the science of evaluations is not currently mature enough to make confident predictions about the precise buffer we should require between current models and a Capability Threshold.
paraphrase: Evaluation science is not yet mature enough to confidently prescribe a precise buffer between current models and a Capability Threshold, though this remains an aspiration.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
excerpt: More outcome-focused safeguard requirements: We have updated our ASL-3 safeguards requirements to be less prescriptive and more outcome-focused.
paraphrase: ASL-3 safeguard requirements were updated to be less prescriptive and more outcome-focused.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
excerpt: Rather than detailing specific operational and technical safeguards, we now specify the overall security or deployment standards and requirements for meeting them.
paraphrase: Instead of detailing specific safeguards, overall security/deployment standards and their requirements are now specified.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / More outcome-focused safeguard requirements
excerpt: This is to allow us to adapt our safeguards more flexibly as our understanding of risks and possible safeguards improves.
paraphrase: The outcome-focused approach allows more flexible safeguard adaptation as understanding improves.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
excerpt: Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models: We have clarified which actors are in and out of scope for the ASL-3 Security Standard.
paraphrase: The scope of actors covered by the ASL-3 Security Standard was clarified.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
excerpt: We also removed the commitment to protect against scaled attacks and distillation attacks from the ASL-2 Security standard.
paraphrase: The commitment to protect against scaled and distillation attacks was removed from the ASL-2 Security Standard.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Clarified ASL-3 and ASL-2 security threat models
excerpt: While distillation remains a concern for more capable models, models stored under ASL-2 safeguards have not yet reached potentially harmful Capability Thresholds.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users
excerpt: Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users: We have updated the ASL-3 Deployment Standard to allow for different levels of safeguards based on deployment context.
paraphrase: The ASL-3 Deployment Standard was updated to allow safeguard levels to vary by deployment context.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / Clarified requirements for deployments with trusted users
excerpt: For any general access systems, we still require passing intensive red-teaming. For internal use, safety testing and deployments to sufficiently trusted users, we will instead require a combination of access controls and monitoring.
paraphrase: General access systems still require intensive red-teaming, while internal use and trusted-user deployments instead require access controls and monitoring.

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / New Capability and Safeguards Reports

locator: Changelog / October 15, 2024 / New Capability and Safeguards Reports
excerpt: We expect that aggregating all the available evidence about model capabilities will provide decision makers with a more complete picture of the overall level of risk and improve our ability to solicit feedback on our work.

excerpt: RSP-2025: This update clarifies which Capability Thresholds would require enhanced safeguards beyond our current ASL-3 standards.
paraphrase: The 2025 update clarifies which Capability Thresholds require safeguards beyond the current ASL-3 standard.

excerpt: New Capability Thresholds: We have added a new capability threshold related to CBRN development, which defines capabilities that could substantially uplift the development capabilities of moderately resourced state programs.
paraphrase: A new CBRN-related capability threshold was added defining substantial uplift to moderately resourced state programs.

excerpt: We have also disaggregated our existing AI R&D capability thresholds, separating them into two distinct levels (the ability to fully automate entry-level AI research work, and the ability to cause dramatic acceleration in the rate of effective scaling) and provided additional detail on the corresponding Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: Existing AI R&D thresholds were split into two levels—full automation of entry-level research and dramatic scaling acceleration—with added detail on Required Safeguards.

excerpt: Iterative Commitment: We have adopted a general commitment to reevaluate our Capability Thresholds whenever we upgrade to a new set of Required Safeguards.
paraphrase: Anthropic commits to reevaluating Capability Thresholds each time Required Safeguards are upgraded.

excerpt: We have decided not to maintain a commitment to define ASL-N+1 evaluations by the time we develop ASL-N models; such an approach would add unnecessary complexity because Capability Thresholds do not naturally come grouped in discrete levels.
paraphrase: Anthropic dropped the commitment to pre-define next-level evaluations by the time current-level models are developed, since thresholds do not group into discrete levels naturally.

excerpt: We believe it is more practical and sensible instead to commit to reconsidering the whole list of Capability Thresholds whenever we upgrade our safeguards.
paraphrase: Anthropic prefers reconsidering the entire list of Capability Thresholds whenever safeguards are upgraded, as more practical.
